==English== {{wp}} ===Pronunciation=== * {{IPA|en|/ˈðeɪ̯/|a=RP,GA}} ** {{audio|en|En-uk-they.ogg|a=RP}} ** {{audio|en|En-us-they.ogg|a=GA}} * {{IPA|en|[ˈðæ̝ɪ̯]|a=AU}} * {{IPA|en|/ðə/|a=Northumbrian,unstressed}} * {{rhymes|en|eɪ|s=1}} * {{hyph|en|they}} * {{hmp|en|day|the|aa1=th-stopping|aa2=Northumbria}} ===Etymology 1=== {{etymon|en|id=pronoun|:inh|enm:þei|tree=1}} {{word|en|ine|só}} From {{inh|en|enm|þei}}, borrowed in the 1200s from {{der|en|non|þeir}},{{R:American Heritage Dictionary}} plural of the demonstrative {{m|non|sá}} which acted as a plural pronoun. Displaced native {{ncog|enm|he}} from {{ncog|ang|hīe}} — which vowel changes had left indistinct from {{m|enm|he|t=he}} — by the 1400s,{{R:Etymonline}}Otto Jespersen, ''Growth and Structure of the English Language'' being readily incorporated alongside native words beginning with the same sound ({{m|en|the}}, {{m|en|that}}, {{m|en|this}}). Used as a singular pronoun since 1300, e.g. in the 1325 ''Cursor Mundi''. The Norse term (whence also {{cog|is|þeir|t=they}}, {{cog|fo|teir|t=they}}, {{cog|da|de|t=they}}, {{cog|sv|de|t=they}}, {{cog|nn|dei|t=they}}) is from {{der|en|gem-pro|*þai|t=those}} (from {{der|en|ine-pro|*só|*to-|that}}), whence also {{cog|ang|þā|t=those}} (whence obsolete English {{dbt|en|tho|notext=1}}), {{cog|sco|thae}}, {{m|sco|thai}}, {{m|sco|thay|t=they; those}}, {{cog|swg|dia|t=they}}. The origin of the determiner {{m|en|they|t=the, those}} is unclear. The ''OED'', ''English Dialect Dictionary'' and ''Middle English Dictionary''{{R:MED Online|entry=thei|pos=pron|id=MED45106|accessdate=2016-01-28}} define it and its Middle English predecessor {{m|enm|thei}} as a demonstrative determiner or adjective meaning “those” or “the”. This could be a continuation of the use of the English pronoun {{m|en|they}}'s Old Norse etymon {{m|non|þeir}} as a demonstrative meaning “those”, but the ''OED'' and ''EDD'' say it is limited to southern, especially southwestern, England, specifically outside the region of Norse contact. ====Pronoun==== {{en-pron|desc=third-person, nominative case, usually plural, sometimes singular|objective case|them|possessive|their|possessive noun|theirs|reflexive|themselves|or reflexive singular|themself}} # {{senseid|en|third-person plural nominative}} {{lb|en|the third-person plural nominative}} A group of entities previously mentioned. {{defdate|since 13th c.}} #: {{ux|en|Fred and Jane? '''They''' just arrived.}} #: {{ux|en|Dogs may bark if '''they''' want to be fed.}} #: {{ux|en|Plants wilt if '''they''' are not watered.}} #: {{ux|en|I have a car and a truck, but '''they''' are both broken.}} #* {{quote-book|en|year=1620|section=Nouell 8, The Eighth Day|title= {{w|The Decameron|The Decameron, Containing an Hundred Pleaſant Nouels: Wittily Diſcourſed, Betweene Seuen Honourable Ladies, and Three Noble Gentlemen}} |author= w:Giovanni Bocaccio|tlr= w:John Florio |publisher=Isaac Iaggard|url= https://books.google.co.nz/books?id=FEz6_FECCI0C |passage={{...}}purſued his vnneighbourly purpoſe in ſuch ſort: that hee being the ſtronger perſwader, and ſhe (belike) too credulous in beleeuing or elſe ouer-feeble in reſiſting, from priuate imparlance, '''they''' fell to action; and continued their cloſe fight a long while together, vnſeene and vvithout ſuſpition, no doubt to their equall ioy and contentment.}} #* {{quote-book|en|year=2010|title=Iguana Invasion!: Exotic Pets Gone Wild in Florida|page=9|isbn=1561644684 |passage=There is no reason to be scared of iguanas. '''They''' do not attack humans.}} # {{senseid|en|third-person singular nominative}} {{lb|en|the third-person singular nominative|occasionally|proscribed}} A single person, previously mentioned, whose [[gender]] is unknown, irrelevant, or [[non-binary]]. ## One whose gender is unknown, irrelevant, or both. {{defdate|since 14th c.}} ##: {{ux|en|Somebody requested a seat at Friday's performance but didn't say if '''they''' preferred the balcony or the floor. Some States Are Offering a Nonbinary Option|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2019/05/29/us/nonbinary-drivers-licenses.html|date=2019-05-29|passage=Ever since El Martinez started asking to be called by the gender-neutral pronouns “they/them” in the ninth grade, '''they''' have fielded skepticism in a variety of forms and from a multitude of sources about what it means to identify as nonbinary.|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20190608042105/https://www.nytimes.com/2019/05/29/us/nonbinary-drivers-licenses.html}} ##* {{see more citations|en}} # {{senseid|en|indefinite}} {{lb|en|indefinite pronoun, vague meaning}} People; some people; people in general; someone, excluding the speaker. #: {{cot|en|[[one#Pronoun|one]]|generic you}} #: {{ux|en|'''They''' say it’s a good place to live.}} #: {{ux|en|'''They''' didn’t have computers in the old days.}} #: {{ux|en|'''They''' built this city on rock and roll.}} #: {{coi|en|[[they don't make them like they used to|'''They''' don’t make them like '''they''' used to]].}} #* {{RQ:en:New York Times|date=February 16, 1986|author=w:William Safire|title=On Language; Moon Of My Delight|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20150524191416/https://www.nytimes.com/1986/02/16/magazine/on-language-moon-of-my-delight.html|archivedate=May 24, 2015|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1986/02/16/magazine/on-language-moon-of-my-delight.html|section=Section 6 / Magazine|page=10|text=Always get a second source, '''they''' tell us in investigative lexicography;{{...}}}} #* {{quote-song|en|year=2002|author=w:Linda Perry|title={{w|Beautiful (Christina Aguilera song)|Beautiful}}|album=Stripped|artist=w:Christina Aguilera|passage=I am beautiful, no matter what '''they''' say}} #* {{RQ:Wired |date=2025-03-11 |author=Lauren Smiley |title=The Worst 7 Years in Boeing’s History—and the Man Who Won’t Stop Fighting for Answers. Fatal crashes. A door blowout. Grounded planes. Inside the citizen-led, obsessive campaign to hold Boeing accountable and prevent the next disaster |url=https://www.wired.com/story/boeing-whistleblower-737-max/ |passage=Hurtling through the air that evening in seat 10C, I read the US House committee’s Max investigation, a disruptor of illusions. Like many fliers, I’d long ago made my bargain with risk. I’d taken comfort in statistics, summoned faith in the engineers and assembly workers, the pilots, the system. I’d shunted away the knowledge—paralyzing, if you let it in—that stepping on an airplane is an extraordinary act of trust. Deep in the report, I reached the part about a senior manager at Boeing’s factory in Renton, a guy named Ed Pierson, who seemingly knew what we all know when we soothe ourselves by thinking, '''''They''' wouldn’t let it fly if it weren’t safe.'' We’re all relying on someone to be the “'''they'''.”|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20260727133926/https://www.wired.com/story/boeing-whistleblower-737-max/|archivedate=27 July 2026}} # {{senseid|en|indefinite}} {{lb|en|indefinite pronoun}} The authorities, the (power) elites, the [[powers that be]], the [[establishment]], [[the man]], the [[system]]: government, police, employers, etc. #: {{ux|en|'''They''''ll tax us for the air we breathe next.}} #: {{ux|en|'''They''' should increase our wages.}} #: {{ux|en|Ha, you believe the moon is real? That's just what '''they''' want you to think.}} # {{lb|en|bridge}} The opponents of the side which is [[keep score|keeping score]]. #: {{ant|en|we}} =====Usage notes===== * {{sense|singular pronoun}} Usage of ''they'' as a singular pronoun began in the 1300s and has been common ever since, despite attempts by some grammarians, beginning in 1795,Anne Bodine, ''Androcentrism in Prescriptive Grammar: Singular 'they', Sex-indefinite 'he', and 'he or she''', in ''Language in Society'', v. 4 (1975), pages 129–146 to condemn it as a violation of traditional ([[Latinate]]) agreement rules. Some other grammarians have countered that criticism since at least 1896.William Malone Baskervill and James Witt Sewell's ''An English Grammar'' (1896) says singular ''they'' is "frequently found ''when the antecedent includes or implies both genders''. The masculine does not really represent a feminine antecedent"; it furthermore recommends changing it to ''he'' or ''she'' "''unless both genders are implied''". (Italics in original.) ''Fowler's Modern English Usage'' (third edition) notes that it "is being left unaltered by copy editors" and is "not widely felt to lie in a prohibited zone". Some authors compare use of singular ''they'' to widespread use of singular ''you'' instead of ''thou''.Michael Reed, ''Tech Book 1'' {{ISBN|0956081312}}, ''Note about pronoun usage'', page 9: "Singular ''they'' can introduce some ambiguity because the antecedent of the pronoun “they” could theoretically be a male or female [... but] English has survived the loss of pronouns such as ''thou'' (singular ''you'') despite the consequent potential for ambiguity."John McWhorter, ''Word on the Street: Debunking the Myth of a Pure Standard'' (2009, {{ISBN|0786731478}}: "In this light, our modern grammarians' discomfort with singular ''they'' is nothing but this comical intermediate stage in an inevitable change, as misguided and futile as the old grumbles about singular ''you''." See {{w|singular they|Wikipedia's article on singular ''they''}} for more; see also the usage notes about {{m|en|themself}}. (Compare {{m|en|he}}.) * {{sense|singular pronoun}} In the past, ''they'' tended to be used of a generic or unidentified person, or someone who was not previously named or identified as male or female. It has increasingly been used to refer to an unnamed person even if the gender of the person is known. * {{sense|singular pronoun}} Even when used as a singular pronoun, in standard English singular ''they'' uses the same verb conjugations as plural ''they'', like singular and plural ''you'': "George, you ''were'' {{small|[not ''was'']}} here when the masked figure ran past, ''were'' {{small|[not ''was'']}} they wearing red or blue?" * {{sense|singular pronoun}} Infrequently, ''they'' is used of an individual person of known, binary gender. See [[Citations:they#Pronoun: single person of specified sex or gender|citations]]. * {{sense|singular pronoun}} Infrequently, ''they'' is used of an individual animal which would more commonly be referred to as ''[[it]]''. See [[Citations:they#Pronoun: single animal or plant|citations]]. * {{sense|indefinite pronoun}} ''[[one|One]]'' is also an indefinite pronoun, but the two words do not mean the same thing and are rarely interchangeable. "They" refers to people in general (hence the expressions {{m|en|they say}}, {{m|en|so they say}}, {{m|en|you know what they say}}), whereas "one" refers to one person (often such that what is true for that person is true for everyone). ''You'' may also be used to refer to people in general; such use of that pronoun is called the [[generic you#Noun|generic ''you'']]. *: ''They say beauty is in the eye of the beholder.'' *: ''One may say, "Beauty is in the eye of the beholder."'' *: ''You may say, "Beauty is in the eye of the beholder."'' =====Alternative forms===== * {{alt|en|They}} {{q|honorific}} * {{alt|en|dey}}
